hook: A massive object 630 million years after the Big Bang defies expectations.

sections.voiceover: A massive object 630 million years after the Big Bang defies expectations.
sections.visual_cue: CGI animation of an ancient, glowing quasar emitting intense light against a dark, early universe background.
sections.sfx_cue: Deep, resonant space hum transitioning into a sharp, clear chime.
b_roll: CGI visualization of an early universe quasar

sections.voiceover: In July 2026, the European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope detected 31 distant quasars. How did such a giant form so early?
sections.visual_cue: Split screen showing the Euclid space telescope logo and a data visualization of the quasar's mass.
b_roll: Data chart representing 360 million solar masses

sections.voiceover: But this discovery breaks the Euclid space telescope's record by peering back an additional 40 million years.
sections.visual_cue: Visual timeline graphic showing the shift in the observation record.
b_roll: Timeline graphic of space exploration records

sections.voiceover: Julien Wolf led Euclid Consortium astronomers at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Heidelberg, Germany. The Euclid space telescope reveals this 360 million solar mass giant defies our current growth models.
sections.visual_cue: Portrait of Julien Wolf overlaid with the Max Planck Institute logo and a simulated galactic core.
b_roll: Computer simulation of a galactic core

sections.voiceover: We are now seeing the universe as it was 630 million years old.
sections.visual_cue: Wide-angle cinematic shot of the deep, star-filled cosmos.
